title: A quantum double-bracket algorithm for imaginary-time evolution with exponentially shorter depth
abstract: Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) is a widely used technique for preparing the ground state of a target Hamiltonian. Building on the recently proposed framework of Double-Bracket quantum ITE (DB-QITE), we introduce a probabilistic variant (PDBQITE) that achieves an exponential reduction in circuit depth. Our algorithm requires only a single ancilla qubit and a quantum circuit that consists of one controlled real-time evolution and one mid-circuit measurement per iteration. The trade-off is an exponential decay of the total success probability with the number of iterations, for which we derive an analytical lower bound that is independent of system size. Our numerical simulations show that the per-step success probability remains close to unity, making it realistic to execute many iterations, thus providing a substantial improvement over prior constructions. We show that PDBQITE outperforms the near-term probabilistic algorithm PITE for ground-state preparation of molecular Hamiltonians, and that a hybrid QAOA-PDBQITE scheme achieves higher approximation ratios than QAOA at the same circuit depth on random regular graphs for the MaxCut problem.
summary: This paper presents PDBQITE, a novel, depth-efficient quantum algorithm for performing imaginary-time evolution to find ground states. By replacing the exponentially deep circuit of previous methods with a probabilistic, linear combination approach, it significantly reduces circuit depth. The algorithm is shown to outperform existing techniques on molecular Hamiltonians and optimization problems like MaxCut.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently preparing the ground state of a target Hamiltonian using Imaginary-Time Evolution (ITE) with significantly reduced quantum circuit depth compared to prior methods.
main_result: The proposed PDBQITE algorithm achieves an exponential reduction in circuit depth compared to DB-QITE, and hybrid QAOA-PDBQITE schemes outperform standard QAOA for optimization problems like MaxCut.
method: It introduces PDBQITE, a probabilistic variant of Double-Bracket QITE, which approximates the non-unitary ITE evolution by applying a linear combination of unitaries at each step.
model_or_system: The core model is the quantum state evolution governed by the imaginary-time evolution operator $e^{-H	au}$. Applications include finding the ground state of molecular Hamiltonians (e.g., LiH, BeH2) and solving combinatorial optimization problems like MaxCut and MIS.
key_observables: Approximation ratio (fidelity to the ground state), per-step success probability, and energy expectation values.
important_parameters: Number of iterations ($K$), time step size ($\sqrt{s}$), and the system size ($n$ qubits).
main_assumptions: The primary trade-off is the exponential decay of the total success probability, although an analytical lower bound independent of system size is derived.
figures_summary: Figures compare the approximation ratio vs. QAOA depth for MaxCut, show the energy trajectory and cumulative probability of success for molecular Hamiltonians ($	ext{BeH}_2$, $	ext{LiH}$), and compare PDBQITE performance against PITE.
paper_structure: The paper introduces ITE and DB-QITE, details the implementation and theory of PDBQITE, evaluates its performance on MaxCut and molecular Hamiltonians, and concludes with a summary of the improved resource scaling.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, resource-efficient quantum algorithm for simulating fundamental quantum dynamics (ground state preparation) that directly addresses the depth scaling bottleneck in quantum simulation algorithms.

figures.caption: Figure 1: General overview of our method. At first the total evolution time τ is discretized into K steps. Then, the quantum circuit Vk corresponding to each step of the algorithm is constructed by measuring the overlap ⟨ψ0| e−i(k+1)√sH |ψ0⟩, where |ψ0⟩is the initial state. Provided that we measure the ancilla in the state |0⟩at every step of the algorithm, then at step K we will have an approximation of the ITE state.

Figure 2: Energy trajectory (left figure) and cumulative probability of success (right figure) for the LiH molecule. For first-order PDBQITE we choose a timestep sk = 0.2 and perform 10 iterations, while for second-order PDBQITE and PITE we choose a timestep sk = 0.7 and perform only 5 iterations. Horizontal lines mark the cumulative success probability at which second-order (dotted) and first-order (dashed) PDBQITE reach chemical accuracy.

Figure 3: Approximation ratio (left) and cumulative success probability (right) as a function of “equivalent QAOA layers”, for randomly weighted 4-regular MaxCut instances of size n = 18. We compare QAOA against QAOA augmented with up to three PDBQITE steps of first (s = 0.35) and second order (s = 0.7).
